title: Why Distributed Systems Are Hard
summary: Why partial failure, unreliable networks, ambiguous timeouts, partitions and split brain make multi-machine systems fundamentally harder than one computer.

questions.prompt: What is a *partial failure*, and why is it the defining problem of distributed systems compared to a program on one machine?
questions.hint: On one machine a crash is usually total. What can one node know about another?
keyPoints: Partial failure: some components fail or are slow while others keep working
On a single machine, failures tend to be total and obvious (crash and restart)
Nodes only learn about each other through messages that can be lost, delayed or duplicated
A node often can't tell whether another node is dead, slow, or the network is broken

questions.prompt: Your order service calls the payment service to charge a card and gets a timeout after 3 seconds. A teammate suggests: "On timeout, just call charge again." What could go wrong, and what would you do instead?
questions.hint: List what might have happened on the payment side when you got no reply.
keyPoints: A timeout is ambiguous: the request may have been lost, still in progress, or completed with a lost response
Blind retry can double-charge the customer
Not retrying can leave the order unpaid
Use an idempotency key so the payment service deduplicates retries, then retry with backoff
Optionally query the payment status by that key before retrying / reconcile later

questions.prompt: (a) Each of your 2,000 servers is independently up 99.95% of the time. What's the probability that **all** are up at a given moment? (b) A page request fans out to 50 backend calls in parallel; each call has a 2% chance of being slower than 1 second. What fraction of page loads will be slower than 1 second?
questions.hint: P(all fine) = p^n. P(at least one bad) = 1 − P(all fine). `ln(0.9995) ≈ −0.0005`, `0.98^50 ≈ 0.364`.
keyPoints: (a) So about 63% of the time at least one server is down: failure is the normal state
(b) About 64% of page loads are slow because fan-out amplifies tail latency
questions.answer:
(a) `0.9995^2000 = e^(2000 × ln 0.9995) ≈ e^(-1.0) ≈ 0.37`. About 37% of the time everything is up; 63% of the time something is down.

(b) `1 − 0.98^50 ≈ 1 − 0.364 = 0.636`, so roughly 64% of page loads exceed 1 s, even though each backend is slow only 2% of the time.

questions.prompt: Explain split brain in a leader–follower database. Then explain how a majority quorum and fencing tokens each help prevent damage.
questions.hint: What does the follower conclude when heartbeats stop? What if the old leader was only paused?
keyPoints: During a partition (or leader pause), a follower may promote itself while the old leader still believes it leads; two leaders accept conflicting writes
Majority quorum: a leader needs votes from more than half the nodes, and only one side of a partition can have a majority
Fencing tokens: each new leader gets a strictly increasing epoch/term number
Storage rejects writes with an older token, so a zombie old leader (e.g. after a GC pause) can't overwrite newer data
Even with quorums, a paused old leader may still try to act, which is why fencing is needed

questions.prompt: Your API calls a recommendations service with **no timeout**. One afternoon, the recommendations service starts responding in 60+ seconds. Within minutes your whole API is down, even for endpoints that don't use recommendations. Explain the chain of events and three fixes.
questions.hint: What resources does a waiting request hold onto?
keyPoints: Requests waiting on the slow dependency hold threads/connections/memory, which pile up until the pool is exhausted
Then all endpoints fail because no workers are free: a cascading failure
Fix 1: timeouts on every remote call (set slightly above the dependency's p99)
Fix 2: circuit breaker / bulkheads (separate pools) so one dependency can't consume everything
Fix 3: graceful degradation, e.g. render the page without recommendations or with a cached fallback

questions.prompt: You run one primary database in data center A with a replica in data center B, and an automatic failover script: "if B can't reach A for 10 seconds, promote B." Critique this design and propose a safer one.
questions.hint: What happens if only the A–B link breaks, but clients can still reach A? How many observers should vote?
keyPoints: A broken A–B link (partition) makes B promote itself while A is still alive and serving clients: split brain
A long GC pause or slow network can also trigger false failover
Use an odd number of voters (e.g. a third site or a 3/5-node consensus system like etcd/ZooKeeper) and require a majority to elect a leader
Old leader must step down when it loses quorum (lease that expires), and writes carry fencing tokens/epochs
Mention that async replication means failover may lose recent writes; pick timeouts that balance false positives vs downtime
